“Be very clear-eyed. Be very aware of what information you are able to expect in return for what you are sharing, and start to build a foundation,” said Caroline Zier, OpenAI’s deputy lead for national security, during a discussion at the Hudson Institute.

articles.title_orig: War, tariffs and China: What the US midterms mean for the Asia-Pacific
articles.title_zh: War, tariffs and China: What the US midterms mean for the Asia-Pacific
articles.content_orig:
Xi urges diplomacy on Iran as Oman’s sultan makes historic visit to China
Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia – Across the Asia-Pacific region, governments and businesses reeling from the energy shock of the United States and Israel’s war on Iran are watching Tuesday’s US midterm elections closely.
Many want to see “enormous changes” during the rest of President Donald Trump’s term, analysts say, from the war on Iran to his policies on trade and tariffs. But few expect that to happen, even with the Democrats poised to take the House of Representatives, and potentially the Senate, from Trump’s Republican Party.
“Of course, everybody is watching,” said Steven Okun, a trade specialist and the chief executive of APAC Advisors, a Singapore-based consulting firm. “It’s great political theatre.”
Outside the Middle East, no region has been hit harder by the war on Iran than the Asia-Pacific. Before the start of the conflict in January, the region took in most of the Gulf oil and gas that passed through the Strait of Hormuz.
When Iran closed the chokepoint in response to the US and Israel’s strikes, much of the region was left facing shortages .
The Philippines, which relies on the Gulf for more than 90 percent of its crude oil imports, has been under a national energy emergency since March. Soaring fuel costs have drained the foreign exchange reserves of the region’s poorest economies – Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar and East Timor, according to the Institute of Southeast Asian Studies (ISEAS)-Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore. Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and Vietnam have also spent heavily on fuel subsidies to shield consumers, it said.
Public opinion in the Asia-Pacific region remains firmly opposed to the war, but Okun said a Democratic-controlled US Congress was unlikely to force Trump to end the eight-month conflict.
“With Iran, I don’t see [a Democrat-controlled Congress] having much change at all, other than the fact that the war will be investigated and there will be oversight hearings,” Okun told Al Jazeera. “We might even see an impeachment of the secretary of defence, but it doesn’t change the overall impact of the war.”
Under the US Constitution, Congress holds the power to formally declare war, but Trump has claimed the attacks on Iran were in self-defence and has so far ignored congressional resolutions directing him to withdraw US forces from hostilities. If a Democrat-controlled Congress passes legislation restricting military operations or cutting funding for them, Trump can veto it. Overriding a veto requires a two-thirds majority in both chambers, which Democrats are almost certain to fall short of.
On trade and tariffs, too, analysts see little room for Congress to rein in Trump.
The US president rattled global markets last year when he imposed “reciprocal” tariffs of 10 percent to 50 percent on some 90 countries, with the aim of shrinking the US trade deficit. Asia was again hit harder than most. Cambodia faced a 49 percent tariff and Laos 48 percent. Vietnam was slapped with 46 percent and Myanmar 45 percent.
After the Supreme Court struck down those tariffs in February, the Trump administration turned to other tools . In July, it imposed tariffs of 10 percent and 12.5 percent on goods from 60 trading partners, accusing them of failing to stop imports made with forced labour . In Asia, the list includes China, Japan, South Korea and seven Southeast Asian nations – Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
“In some ways, the new Congress is not going to matter to the Asia Pacific because it’s not going to affect trade policy,” Okun said. “Congress cannot change that … Tariffs don’t change. The war doesn’t change.”
Still, some analysts see a narrow opening.
Stephen Olson, a visiting fellow at the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute, argued in a recent essay that a “strong rebuke of ‘Trumpism’” at the polls could embolden a pro-free-trade wing of the Republican Party that has been “intimidated into standing down during the Trump presidency”.
That, Olson wrote, offers “a glimmer of hope” for Southeast Asian countries that depend on the US market. A Democratic-controlled Congress, he said, could also push for carve-outs and exceptions that would give the region’s exporters “a modicum of relief”. But any deeper shift in US trade policy, he added, will have to wait for the 2028 presidential election.
Joshua Kurlantzick, a senior fellow for Southeast Asia and South Asia at the Council on Foreign Relations, said the region’s wish list goes beyond trade to security.
“I think nearly all of Asia would like to see enormous changes, across many domains, during the rest of Trump’s term,” he told Al Jazeera. “But I think much of the region believes this will not happen.”
Besides “more stability” in trade and tariff policy, Asia-Pacific countries “would like to feel more stable in security guarantees from the US,” he said. They would also like a “more clear, obvious US presence” in the South China Sea , where China’s claims overlap with those of five Southeast Asian nations, and in the Taiwan Strait , which separates China from Taiwan , the self-governed island Beijing claims as its territory.
Businesses will also be watching whether a major Republican loss leads to “greater GOP willingness in Congress to stand up to Trump, along with Democrats, on issues important to companies in Asia,” Kurlantzick said, including tariffs, trade policy, arms sales and “overall economic unpredictability”.
One area where analysts do expect some change is US policy on Chinese technology.
The new Congress, whichever party controls it, will pass tougher restrictions on China, said Okun at APAC Advisors.
These include the Remote Access Security Act, which would extend export controls to remote access of US goods, software or technology and the Chip Security Act, which would require companies to verify that advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips remain in authorised locations, to prevent diversion to foreign adversaries. It also includes the Multilateral Alignment of Technology Controls on Hardware Act, known as the MATCH Act, which would press allies to bring their controls on chipmaking equipment in line with Washington’s, to keep advanced chipmaking technology out of China’s hands.
“The next Congress is going to pass them regardless of midterms because both parties agree on them,” Okun said. “The person who is least restrictive now on China is the US president,” he added, referring to Trump’s courting of China’s President Xi Jinping.
The two men have met twice this year as ties have warmed after a bitter and costly trade war last year. To preserve the fragile trade truce, Trump has also held off approving a $14bn package of arms sales to Taiwan, which would be the largest ever for Taipei.
Some analysts meanwhile worry that a lame-duck Trump, hemmed in at home by a Democratic Congress, could turn more forcefully to foreign policy.
“We should not be surprised by continued erratic foreign policy,” said James Guild, an assistant professor at the Indonesian International Islamic University.
“The Democrats have a poor record of effectively opposing and holding Trump accountable using conventional tools of congressional oversight,” Guild said. “We will have to wait and see if they rise to the moment this time.”

articles.title_orig: Gas prices are set to be highest for any Election Day in U.S. history
articles.title_zh: Gas prices are set to be highest for any Election Day in U.S. history
articles.content_orig:
Petrol prices have dipped amid renewed diplomatic efforts to end the US-Israel war on Iran, but remain high ahead of the United States midterm elections , as the cost of living remains a central issue for voters.
On Monday, the average price for a gallon (3.78 litres) of regular petrol was $4.17, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), which tracks daily petrol prices. That is down 12 cents from this time last week and 23 cents from a month ago.
By comparison, prices were $3.04 this time a year ago and $2.98 on February 28, when the US and Israel first struck Iran.
Diesel fuel prices remain high at $6.29 per gallon, but that is down 6 cents from this time last week. Diesel prices climbed above $6 a gallon for the first time in September before topping out at $6.53.
The average petrol price of President Donald Trump’s second term to date was set to exceed $3.46 a gallon on Monday, surpassing the previous record for a presidential administration set under former President Joe Biden, according to a Financial Times analysis of federal data.
Oil prices are continuing to fall, down 6 percent on Monday as diplomatic efforts to end the US-Israel war on Iran continued following in-person talks in Qatar over the weekend.
“Oil markets down significantly this morning after Trump signalled he favoured negotiations and not new attacks on Iran,” Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, said in a post on X. “Oil down [approximately] 5%, wholesale gasoline and diesel pointing to roughly 16 [cents per gallon] decline. The national average could fall under $4 a gallon in the next week barring a course change.”
Cost-of-living issues remain top of mind for US voters as they head to the polls. An Associated Press-NORC poll last month found that a majority of Americans believe addressing cost-of-living issues should be a priority for Congress, including 78 percent of Republicans and 89 percent of Democrats.
“Once this conflict comes to an end, gas prices will drop drastically, and the Iranian terrorist regime will not have a nuclear weapon,” White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers told Al Jazeera. “Protecting America’s national security from threats by a radical terrorist regime that has chanted ‘Death to America’ for 47 years was the right thing to do – and President Trump is the only president who has had the courage to do it.”
Rogers added, “Thanks to the exceptional work of the US military, more oil is now flowing out of the Persian Gulf than before the Iran conflict began.”
On Wall Street, oil and gas giant stocks were trending downward in midday trading. ConocoPhillips was down 3.7 percent, Chevron 2.3 percent and ExxonMobil 3.3 percent.
The major US indices more broadly were in positive territory. The Nasdaq was up 0.7 percent, the S&P 500 0.6 percent and the Dow Jones Industrial Average 1 percent.

articles.title_orig: CNBC's The China Connection newsletter: Nvidia's humanoid push relies on China-made robot hands
articles.title_zh: CNBC's The China Connection newsletter: Nvidia's humanoid push relies on China-made robot hands
articles.content_orig:
Hi, this is Evelyn, writing to you from Beijing. Welcome to the latest edition of The China Connection — a snapshot of what I'm seeing and hearing from local businesses.
Chinese robot companies still underpin many U.S. tech endeavors, especially when it comes to the pain point of robotic hands. Who is one of the latest on Nvidia's radar?
In just a few months, Nvidia has showcased two humanoid robot training packages: one with mechanical hands from Sharpa , and another with hands from Wuji .
Both have ties to founders in Shanghai.
Pan Yunzhe founded Wuji in 2019, eventually moving much of the team to Shenzhen and drawing backers such as Ant Group, HSG and Future Capital, according to PitchBook. A demo video last week claimed a Wuji Hand 2 could autonomously spin a pen, despite interference .
The Wuji Hand 2 made it onto a slide Oct. 21 behind Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang as he told a crowd in Berlin about a new humanoid hardware system for training the robots on Nvidia software. The robot body comes from Agile Robots, which has offices in Germany, China and the U.S.
"It will be the flywheel by which we can accelerate development of robotics," Huang said of the hardware system, called Agile One SN. Agile Robots announced the system, which uses Nvidia's Isaac robotics software and Jetson Thor computing platform.
Research institutions, such as Stanford and ETH Zurich, can likely start using the Agile One SN system in early 2027, according to Nvidia .
Stanford and ETH Zurich were also among the institutions Nvidia named in connection with its first reference humanoid design, announced May 31. That system uses a body from Chinese humanoid company Unitree and mechanical hands from Sharpa. It was scheduled for delivery from late 2026.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on whether deliveries had begun, or whether the researchers would try both reference robots, or just one.
Sharpa, headquartered in Singapore, was co-founded by David Li, CEO of Shanghai-based lidar company Hesai . Sharpa has said its manufacturing R&D is in Shanghai .
While these are just two of the many robotic hand makers in China — and globally — they've grown so much in prominence that Google DeepMind research lead Keerthana Gopalakrishnan directly compared the two startups in a podcast last month .
Sharpa Wave is a bit stronger than Wuji, which is closer in size to a typical human hand but has the strength of a ten-year-old, she said. It was not clear whether she was testing the Wuji Hand 2 or an earlier version.
In September, humanoid startup JoyIn's Zhu Mingxuan told me she found Wuji's mechanical hands very light and very good at completing tasks, but prone to heating up while doing so. She said Sharpa's performed better, but were far more expensive.
Hardware is limiting humanoid development, and hands are the main challenge, she said. Zhu said she left U.S. humanoid company Figure last year, where she had also worked on models to help humanoid robots mimic human actions.
As China pushes its humanoid industry to develop more core technologies , mechanical hands are one way companies can try to stand out in the robot race.
Consumer electronics company Xiaomi said last week that, by testing its robotic hand in its car factory, it found that most of the tasks it tested required only a specific range of movement.
And in another sign of just how far along the tech may have come in China, Meta has worked with Chinese startup Fourier for a humanoid prototype, The Information reported Oct. 31, citing sources. Neither company immediately responded to a request for comment.

Car salesman Li Ke said that, other than the Covid-19 pandemic, the "golden September and silver October" season is the slowest this year he's seen in his 26 years on the job.
China industrial profits see strongest growth since June
Profits at large industrial firms rose 14.4% in September from a year earlier, according to official data .

The company reported a 45% to 50% year-on-year drop in third-quarter revenue , with the Americas and Asia-Pacific seeing the steepest sales drops.

articles.title_orig: Marvell, Lumentum tout historic $115B deal to create ‘category leader’ in AI connectivity
articles.title_zh: Marvell, Lumentum tout historic $115B deal to create ‘category leader’ in AI connectivity
articles.content_orig:
Marvell Technology 's deal for optical components maker Lumentum will create an "enormous" opportunity to address growing connectivity demands from the artificial intelligence infrastructure buildout, Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston told CNBC on Monday.
"You need scale-up technology that needs semiconductors and optical working seamlessly together," Marvell CEO Matt Murphy told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street." "We are going to create a new category of company here."
Since the tie-up is a fixed-ratio deal with no cash, the value will depend on the price of Marvell shares. The company said the transaction has an implied enterprise value of $115 billion for Lumentum, in a release.
Marvell shares slumped 13% in trading Monday, while Lumentum's stock sank nearly 19%. But both stocks have been huge winners in the artificial intelligence boom, with Marvell more than doubling in the past year, prior to Monday's sell-off, and Lumentum quadrupling over that stretch.
Through the acquisition, Marvell said it can combine electrical and optical technologies to meet accelerating and shifting AI connectivity demands across regions and systems. Companies are increasingly relying on optical connections to piece together chips used to run and train large language models.
"We're actually going to create solutions around those that are highly sticky, and the reason that they're sold out is because the demand is exploding, and we don't see that changing anytime soon," Murphy said.
Lumentum shareholders will receive 4.5 Marvell shares for each Lumentum share under the agreement. The deal is expected to close during the first half of 2028.
Marvell's takeover marks one of the most significant bets on AI in 2026 and comes despite recent concerns over the long-term sustainability of infrastructure spending.
This isn't the company's first bet on AI growth. This year, the company closed a multibillion-dollar deal for Celestial AI, a startup focused on optical interconnectivity technology.
Marvell 's Murphy also shot down concerns about Nvidia's circular dealmaking, given the leading AI chipmaker's recent multibillion-dollar investments in both companies.
In a bid to further support the data center infrastructure that houses its AI chips, Nvidia has positioned itself as a central cog in a network of related companies, investing in several technology companies that purchase its chips or neoclouds that rent out computing capacity. That's sparked criticism that companies like Nvidia are virtually funding themselves by taking stakes in customers.
"This is a double down on supporting Nvidia, who is the ecosystem leader in this area," Murphy told CNBC. "We're very committed to that partnership, and I think having two of the key suppliers come together, that support that ecosystem, is going to be a big benefit for them."
Marvell has seen its market value more than triple over the last three years, buoyed by unrelenting AI enthusiasm. Lumentum's stock has more than doubled in 2026 alone.
CORRECTION: This story has been updated to reflect that Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston described the deal as an 'enormous' opportunity. A previous version of this story incorrectly cited the Marvell CEO.

articles.title_orig: Two Chinese Nationals Receive Less Than Three Years Prison Time for Spying on US Navy
articles.title_zh: Two Chinese Nationals Receive Less Than Three Years Prison Time for Spying on US Navy
articles.content_orig:
The pair was accused of gathering information about U.S. military personnel and facilitating secret cash payments.
Two Chinese nationals have been sentenced to 30 months in prison for acting as illegal agents of the People’s Republic of China after conducting surveillance operations targeting U.S. Navy personnel and military facilities.
Their charges are conspiring to act as agents of the PRC government and acting as agents of a foreign government without prior notification to the Attorney General.
One of the convicted criminals, Liren “Ryan” Lai, was arrested in Houston last year.
According to court documents, Lai and co-defendant Yuance Chen of Oregon began acting as agents under a Chinese intelligence officer with PRC’s Ministry of State Security in 2021.
Authorities alleged that the pair photographed U.S. military personnel and facilities, Navy recruiting offices, and naval installations in Washington and California.
They also reportedly attempted to recruit other potential MSS members from the U.S. military.
“Chen and Lai operated as illegal agents for the Chinese government on U.S. soil, carrying out clandestine intelligence work that included making covert payments, collecting sensitive military information, and attempting to recruit American service members,” said Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division.
Their activities included secret “dead drop” cash payments in exchange for intelligence related to the national security of the U.S.
A dead drop of $10,000 was reportedly sent to Chen. The MSS also directed Lai to travel to Phoenix in 2025 to facilitate a cash payment of $20,000.
An unsealed federal affidavit cited an incident that involved Chen surveilling the Naval Special Warfare Command in San Diego, which oversees Navy SEALs.
The pair were arrested on June 27, 2025, in a coordinated FBI counterintelligence and law enforcement operation.
A federal grand jury in the Northern District of California returned an indictment charging both defendants with conspiracy to act as agents of a foreign government without prior notification to the attorney general and acting as agents of a foreign government without prior notification.
Both pleaded guilty and received sentences of 30 months in prison and three years of supervised release.
“Lai’s and Chen’s activities, undertaken at the direction of the PRC, were extensive and brazen. The National Security Division is committed to holding accountable anyone who aids or abets such espionage efforts,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg.
Rozhavsky noted that while “The Chinese government’s efforts to infiltrate our armed forces demonstrate just how far it will go to threaten U.S. national security,” the country has “underestimated the FBI’s commitment to thwarting its illegal activity and holding its agents accountable.”
“Let this sentencing serve as a clear warning: If you attempt to jeopardize the safety and security of our service members, our citizens, or our nation, justice will find you,” added Rozhavsky.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic Investors Push for Cautious Valuation Closer to $1.5 Trillion
articles.title_zh: Anthropic Investors Push for Cautious Valuation Closer to $1.5 Trillion
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic’s quarterly revenue swelled to $17 billion but it still posted a net loss for the latest three months, the artificial intelligence giant said in an updated IPO filing released on Monday.
The San Francisco-based company behind the Claude chatbot also disclosed that it has committed to spend $895.4 billion on AI computing and infrastructure like data centers, including $70 billion that’s due to be spent in the next 12 months.
Watch NBC Bay Area News free wherever you are
The numbers were released about a week after Anthropic issued its original IPO filing in preparation for what’s expected to be a blockbuster Wall Street debut later this month.
The document, like the earlier filing, shows the company’s revenue is growing but — like its AI rivals — profit is still elusive.
Anthropic’s revenue grew by 13 times to $33.2 billion for the first nine months of the year, but it reported a net loss of $104 billion, including a charge of $94 billion for an accounting adjustment related to financing agreements.
On a quarterly basis, Anthropic lost $23.3 billion on revenue of $17 billion.
The filing gave no indication of how much the company ultimately expects to raise, or what the shares will be priced at when it goes public. Anthropic has previously said it will list its stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker symbol “ANT.”

articles.title_orig: Anthropic warns that it’s very close to RSI capability, aka self-building AI
articles.title_zh: Anthropic warns that it’s very close to RSI capability, aka self-building AI
articles.content_orig:

Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE.
While much attention has focused on the updated financials Anthropic revealed in its revised S-1A on Monday, (revenue is soaring, but so are expenses), the AI lab dropped another little bombshell in the fine print.
The filing seems to warn that the company is on the cusp of creating a model capable of recursive self-improvement (RSI).
RSI is the point at which AI grows so good at training itself that it spawns a dramatic acceleration of AI capabilities. To the AI doomers, RSI represents the cataclysm from which there is no return, in which AI builds itself into something powerful enough that it slips beyond human control and may be indifferent to the damage it causes while achieving its goals.
To AI enthusiasts, RSI, or some version of AI reliably using itself to improve, represents the technology’s promise, where it becomes a tool of unimaginable productivity, scientific discovery, and more.
Anthropic seems to believe that RSI is both a promise and a peril. It says in the S-1 that it uses AI in its R&D, but it cautions: “Using AI to help build more capable AI could also pose a considerable safety risk, particularly if it sharply accelerates the pace of progress. This is one of the areas covered by our Responsible Scaling Policy, which sets out our plans to monitor and mitigate the risks as we approach what has been termed ‘recursive self-improvement.’”
When the term RSI became popular earlier this year , many believed it was a buzzword or, at best, a goal too hard to achieve, define, or prove.
But on Monday, Anthropic added new statements to its Risk Factors section, saying 1) it has already used AI to develop new models whose leaps in capability it didn’t recognize at the time, and 2) it may soon meet its own internal definition of RSI (bold emphasis ours, below):
In addition, our increasing use of AI systems to accelerate our own research and development may cause the capabilities of our models to advance more rapidly than our ability to develop, validate, and implement corresponding safety, alignment, and security measures. As a result, we have in the past not identified , and may in the future not identify, a significant acceleration in our rate of development until after it has occurred.
For example, our internal estimates and our expectations regarding future models, rather than our current models, indicate that we may imminently meet our Responsible Scaling Policy’s definition of “dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI.” We have not designated any of our current models as exceeding this threshold, and we continue to assess the underlying data.
However, Anthropic also said in the filing that none of its models have crossed this RSI threshold yet and that it is promising to keep humans in the R&D process for the foreseeable future. “We do not anticipate being able to safely use Claude to fully autonomously design and build successive generations of frontier models without meaningful human supervision or understanding, if and when that becomes technically possible. Accordingly, we are considering updates to our Responsible Scaling Policy to keep humans in control of frontier model development at Anthropic.”
Skeptics might point out that an S-1 functions as both disclosure and marketing, and that claims of being close to a model so powerful that it can build itself could fall into the latter category.
Nevertheless, there’s no question that Claude’s capabilities, especially in terms of coding, math, and cybersecurity, have grow in leaps and bounds this year. If Anthropic thinks the possibility of RSI is close, maybe we should believe it and act — perhaps govern — accordingly.

articles.title_orig: Rivian Stock Can Rise More Than 30%. The R2 Isn’t Just for ‘Tesla Switchers.’
articles.title_zh: Rivian Stock Can Rise More Than 30%. The R2 Isn’t Just for ‘Tesla Switchers.’
articles.content_orig:
Rivian Automotive beat Wall Street's third-quarter earnings expectations as it ramped up production of its new R2 entry-level SUV that the company has promised investors will lead it to profitability.
Here's how Rivian performed in the period ended Sept. 30, compared with average estimates compiled by LSEG:
Shares of Rivian were up roughly 7% during afterhours trading Thursday, after hitting a new 52-week low of $11.38 earlier in the day. The stock closed at $11.45 a share, down 1.9%
The electric vehicle maker also revised its 2026 guidance to mark expected improvements in its vehicle deliveries, pre-tax adjusted earnings and capital expenditures.
The new guidance calls for a pre-tax adjusted loss of between $1.75 billion and $1.85 billion — a $100 million improvement at the midpoint from its prior guidance — vehicle deliveries of between 67,000 and 70,000 units, up from at least 65,000; and capital expenditures of between $1.4 billion and $1.5 billion, $300 million less at the midpoint.
Rivian attributed the improvement in its pre-tax adjusted earnings guidance to better-than-expected revenue related to its sales of regulatory credits, an IEEPA tariff refund receivable in the third quarter and its expected increase in vehicle deliveries.
The R2 — the first deliveries of which arrived to customers in June — has become Rivian's best-selling model and was responsible for "much of the gain quarter-over-quarter," the company said.
Rivian delivered a record 19,248 units from July through September. The company does not disclose deliveries by vehicle.
The EV maker remains unprofitable overall but continued to narrow its losses during the quarter. The company reported a net loss attributable to common stockholders of $913 million, compared with a loss of $1.17 billion during the third quarter of 2025.
Rivian's gross profit, which is closely monitored by investors, was $176 million during the third quarter, up from $24 million a year earlier. Its adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization was a loss of $435 million, a $167 million improvement from the same period last year.
The company reported that its software and services segment continues to grow, generating $605 million in revenue and a gross profit of $256 million, a 42% margin. That compares to its automotive operations, which recorded nearly $1.55 billion in revenue and a gross loss of $80 million.
Also on Thursday, Rivian reiterated that it expects the R2, a smaller and less expensive sibling to its current luxury R1S SUV, to have a positive gross margin by the end of the year. CEO RJ Scaringe has said the company needs to scale beyond current R2 production plans of 160,000 units in order to achieve overall profitability.
"That ramp-up is critical for us getting to positive gross margin on R2 and that ultimately will contribute to positive gross margin for the business," Scaringe told CNBC's Phil LeBeau during an interview Thursday. "We're going to see that through the end of the quarter and the unit economics will continue to grow … into Q1 of next year as well."
Rivian on Thursday said its cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments balance was $5.5 billion, up from $5.3 billion to end the second quarter.

articles.title_orig: Russia kills at least 24 in horrific bombing on Ukraine school
articles.title_zh: Russia kills at least 24 in horrific bombing on Ukraine school
articles.content_orig:
At least 24 people were killed after Russian forces bombed a Ukrainian school on Monday in what President Volodymyr Zelensky slammed as a barbaric “double-tap” strike.
Ukraine’s emergency service confirmed that the Komyshuvakha school targeted in the strike was a building used for distributing humanitarian aid, with two of its rescue workers among the dead.
“After the first air strike, there was a repeat strike with nine more bombs, directly on the shelter where people were gathered,” Zelensky wrote on Telegram.
“The Russians could not have been unaware that every week residents who have remained in Komyshuvakha were receiving assistance right there,” he continued.
“This is yet further proof that Russia does not want any kind of de-escalation , any real justice,” Zelensky added.
Monday’s strike occurred in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region, where officials said that 27 people were still missing in the attack.
Rescue teams are currently trying to reach residents who are believed to still be trapped under the rubble, Zaporizhzhia police said.
The threat of repeated Russian attacks in the region has also complicated the search and rescue efforts, Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi noted.
Zaporizhzhia Regional Military Administration Mykhailo Semikin declared Nov. 3 a day of mourning for the victims of the attack.
The Russian military has yet to comment on the deadly airstrike.
The deadly attack came just a day after a localized cease-fire secured by first lady Melania Trump in Russian-occupied Oleshky.
“After the humanitarian operation in Oleshky, there was a moment when the next steps could have shown that progress toward peace was possible,” Zelensky said.
“With these killings, Russia is sending an entirely opposite signal: Russia is counting on more killings,” he added.

articles.title_orig: Oracle Is Offering $10 Billion of High-Grade Dollar Bonds
articles.title_zh: Oracle Is Offering $10 Billion of High-Grade Dollar Bonds
articles.content_orig:
Oracle filed plans on Monday to issue new stock and more debt to finance its artificial intelligence buildout.
The hyperscaler will sell $10 billion in common stock and $10 billion in senior notes, according to filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. While the fundraising was already outlined at an investor day last week , shares tumbled 8.8% Monday.
"This seems to be exactly what they previewed," said Rob Oliver, senior research analyst at Baird. "So I'm not sure why the market is freaking about it."
Oracle said it plans to use the proceeds for general corporate purposes, which may include capital expenditures, repayments of debt and future investments.
The hyperscaler's stock initially bounced after last Wednesday's investor day, when Oracle also issued a revenue forecast of at least $225 billion for fiscal 2030. At the time Oracle also said it was limiting its additional capital market funding for the fiscal 2027 to 2030 investment cycle to that $20 billion.
"This is a major relief given concerns about the state of debt markets and the cost of capital (although UBS has argued that these debt market concerns have been over-stated)," UBS analyst Karl Keirstead said in a note on Thursday.
Oracle plans to turn to vendor financing, customer-provided hardware and customer prepayments to help it transition to positive free cash flow, which it expects to reach in the second half of 2028.
Stock and bonds in Oracle, co-founded by former CEO Larry Ellison, have been under pressure amid growing investor concerns about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure.
Oracle shares are down 33% in 2026 and 50% over the past 12 months. The yield on its investment-grade 4.95% bond due in 2031 is currently 7.276%.
The sentiment shift is also seen in Oracle's five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default. The spread sits at 292, up 265% in one year. That's more in line with a high-end junk bond rating, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence's Gavan Nolan.
While still an investment-grade credit, Oracle was downgraded by S&P to a BBB- in July, one rating level above high yield. It has $125.34 billion in debt, as of Aug. 31, with the bulk in senior notes.
What ultimately matters for Oracle is execution, Pat Nerney, head of investment solutions at Dynasty Financial Partners, said in an email to CNBC Monday.
"Can they do what they say they are going to do? We view this as the narrative across the AI space," he said. "If this gets executed according to plans laid out, they will be rewarded. If they have to come back to market in the back half of '27 after telling everyone this was the last of the capital needed ... look out."
— CNBC's Seema Mody and Ari Levy contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Ukrainian and Russian emergency alert apps send false warnings after hacks
articles.title_zh: Ukrainian and Russian emergency alert apps send false warnings after hacks
articles.content_orig:
One day after Ukraine's emergency alert system was hacked, President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed that Ukraine hacked Russian systems in retaliation on Nov. 2.
"I underlined it several times that we only respond to their attacks," Zelensky told PBS NewsHour. "So, of course, after the attack, when it was very clear to all our people and for all our personnel, and the intelligence, that it's [Russia's] personal attack against our people, civilians, of course, we responded."
Late on Nov. 1, Ukraine's Air Alert app , which provides vital updates to citizens about incoming Russian strikes, was hacked . False warnings of nuclear, chemical, and street-fighting threats were sent out to the app's users across the nation.
"Hi! A nuclear alert is about to go off all across Ukraine! Don't worry, the Oreshnik is on its way," one of the false warnings read in Russian on the Air Alert app.
In the early hours of Nov. 2, Ukraine's Air Alert app said that operations were gradually being restored while the display of targets was temporarily suspended.
Hours after the false warnings were sent to Ukrainian citizens' phones, Russia's own air raid alert system began to show signs of being compromised.
Messages were sent to users claiming "nuclear warheads" had been "launched across all regions of Russia," and that users should "stock up with food for three weeks" and hide in their basements.
"Attention! The Russian Ministry of Emergency Situations' mobile app has been subjected to a massive cyberattack, allowing attackers to send fake information to the public," the Russian Ministry of Civil Defense, Emergencies and Disaster Relief said in a statement.
The emergency alert hacks mark the latest cyberattacks between Ukraine and Russia.
In September, AI company Anthropic said that Russia has been using Claude AI in cyberattacks against Ukraine and Europe, targeting various government ministries and the WhatsApp accounts of high-level officials.
In April, it was revealed that a Russian-linked group hacked more than 170 email accounts belonging to prosecutors and investigators across Ukraine over several ​months.
"It was a cyber attack," said Zelensky about the air alert system hack. "One of the hundreds and thousands of those made by Russians before on banking systems, on pensions, social support, a lot of different support for civilians. Of course, they want each day to make chaos in Ukraine, in all our cities. It's one of such steps by Russia."

articles.title_orig: Oil prices slide in biggest drop since July on hope for more Iran talks
articles.title_zh: Oil prices slide in biggest drop since July on hope for more Iran talks
articles.content_orig:
Oil prices posted their sharpest drop in three months Monday after a series of headlines about Iran gave investors hope that the Trump administration would find a way to end the conflict without further escalation.
International Brent crude oil fell 7.6% to close the day at $104.77 per barrel, while U.S. crude oil dropped 7.3%, to $96.46 per barrel.
The plunges were the largest one-day drops by percentages since July 27. For both key oil benchmarks, it was the largest single-day drop in dollar terms since April 17.
Earlier Monday, Iran’s IRNA news agency cited the Iranian president’s comments that the supreme leader had “granted the government certain authorities” in relation to “seeking to resolve problems through dialogue” with its “enemies.”
Traders read that as Iran’s choosing to continue diplomatic talks with the U.S. through mediators, rather than escalating the war through further strikes on American allies in the region.
That report followed news Sunday that “Trump, for now, wants to let negotiations play out” with Iran, according to Axios.
After oil prices closed for the day, NBC News asked President Donald Trump whether he was considering striking Iran after the midterms, and twice he replied, “No.”
As Trump’s response circulated online, prices continued their descent.
NBC News has reported that Trump was presented with options to resume major combat operations against Iran. However, officials cautioned at the time that no final decisions about the war had been made.
Energy markets are on edge after multiple reports in the past week suggested that Trump could resume striking Iran after Tuesday’s midterm elections, which could in turn lead Iran to again attack energy assets scattered throughout the Middle East.
Trump took notice of Monday’s drop.
“Oil today is down $10,” Trump told reporters in Washington. “And it’s going to go down a lot further because we’re winning with Iran, easily winning.”
Trump later posted about it on social media , writing: “Iran wants a settlement, as soon as possible. It could happen!”
Still, experts say global energy markets remain exposed to multiple risks.
“A broader conflict resulting in major energy infrastructure damage may spike prices as high as $150” per barrel, Bank of America’s Francisco Blanch wrote in September.
“If skirmishes curbing oil flows continue into year end, Brent could trade in a $95-120” per-barrel range, he wrote.
That leaves open the possibility of more upside to oil prices that have surged all year, pressuring consumers around the world.
Since the Iran war started in late February, global oil prices have risen about 45%.
Another problem facing the U.S. economy is the high price of diesel fuel.
On Monday, diesel futures slid 5.4%, their biggest one-day drop since May 6. But, similar to oil, that benchmark is up almost 110% since the start of the year.
Diesel has had a far more dramatic price rise this year than unleaded gas, as both the Iran war and the Ukraine-Russia war have crimped supply.
Russia has historically been a major exporter of diesel to the world. But Ukrainian strikes have badly damaged its refining capacity.
After a brief halt, Ukraine has resumed attacking Russian diesel refineries in recent days.
Economists have been particularly concerned about the unprecedented rise in diesel prices because of the trickle-down effect higher fuel prices for transporting consumer goods can quickly have on the economy.
As of Monday morning, the average U.S. nationwide diesel price was $6.29 per gallon, up 77% since the start of the year.
Steve Kopack is a senior reporter at NBC News covering business and the economy.
Garrett Haake is NBC News' chief White House correspondent.

articles.title_orig: Iran says contacts over ending war continue after talks finish with no breakthrough
articles.title_zh: Iran says contacts over ending war continue after talks finish with no breakthrough
articles.content_orig:
With little transparency from Washington and warmongering from Tehran, people across the Middle East have been left anxious and confused, scanning for signals on whether the conflict between Iran and the United States will reignite.
Related video above: The ongoing conflict in Iran is impacting U.S. borrowing rates, financial experts say
“The mood has definitely shifted,” a 36-year-old American living in Saudi Arabia told CNN. She plans to leave before Tuesday’s U.S. midterm elections, after which U.S. President Donald Trump has hinted renewed fighting is possible.
“People are more cautious in general, and it feels like a waiting game to see what happens,” she added.
At homes and workplaces across Gulf Arab countries, questions are swirling. Residents are searching for clues that could help them plan for school closures or travel disruptions.
The war began in February when the U.S. and Israel launched strikes on Iran that killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei. It entered its eighth month this week with both sides still locked in a stubborn stalemate, neither making progress diplomatically nor able to break the military impasse.
Trump has offered little clarity on his endgame, oscillating between threats of further strikes and openness to possible diplomacy. Iran has tried to project its own deterrence, claiming it now possesses weaponry capable of striking more targets and inflicting even greater damage than before. Mediation is continuing, but a breakthrough would depend on at least one side breaching its own red lines.
Trump wrote on social media this month that Washington “will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the midterm elections.” The president neither ruled out nor confirmed that strikes would resume afterward, which is part of the reason for the ongoing nerves.
Trump also spoke with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday. The contents of the call were unclear, though Axios, which first reported it, said the conversation concerned Iran.
Asked Sunday about his conversation with Netanyahu, Trump provided no details, saying only that he “had a very good talk” with the prime minister.
“The U.S. has been actively feeding into this regionwide sense of anxiety as it keeps signaling that another round of escalation might be imminent,” Hasan Alhasan, a senior fellow for Middle East policy at the International Institute for Strategic Studies, told CNN. “But it’s becoming difficult to distinguish pressure tactics from genuine signals.”
Adding to a sense that escalation could be imminent, Netanyahu, who partnered with the U.S. in attacking Iran and has been pushing for new strikes, will remain in office despite losing his majority in the recent elections. Negotiations to form a new government in Israel look set to begin in earnest next week, but election results suggest it will be difficult for opposition parties to oust Netanyahu quickly, if at all.
Without clarity, residents in the region often rely on hearsay or search social media for reports on troop movements to determine whether a U.S. strike is imminent.
Over the past month, Iranian military commanders have also intensified a series of public messages claiming that Iran has built up large stockpiles of new weapons, a tactic designed to induce fear among Washington’s allies in the region.
A senior security official in Tehran told CNN that Iran will try to target infrastructure beyond oil facilities in the region, including AI, and warned that if the conflict resumes, it will be a long “war of surprises.” On Saturday, Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei ordered a response “without geographical limitations” to any new threat, an apparent effort to present a leader still yet to be seen in public as playing an active role in military preparations.
Foreign workers drawn to wealthy Gulf Arab states by economic opportunities and a tax-free lifestyle have for decades lived in relative stability in a region mired in conflict. That sense of security was shattered this year after the U.S. and Israel launched the war, prompting Tehran to fire unprecedented barrages of ballistic missiles and drones onto Arab cities, disrupting schools, travel and business and causing multiple casualties.
Yet, despite the war, many residents stayed put, telling CNN they feel confident under the protection of well-armed regional militaries. Practical concerns remain, though.
“I’m actively trying not to think about that happening again because I really don’t want another winter with strikes,” Michelle, a 36-year-old American resident of Abu Dhabi, told CNN. “I’ve always felt safe here… but I’m more concerned that our lives will have to change again.”
This month, people were surprised to learn that families of U.S. diplomats have begun leaving discreetly, with the departures becoming known only after their children started saying goodbye to classmates at school. Many of those leaving had only recently returned to their posts after being ordered out at the height of the Iran war in March, making the exits feel like a frustrating and chaotic déjà vu.
Fueling anxiety among residents are reports of thousands of U.S. troops being dispatched to the region, as reported by the Associated Press.
In Saudi Arabia, where major events have already been canceled and offices closed with staff working remotely after the Iran-allied Houthi rebels intensified strikes, residents told CNN they were concerned that a return to war could increase pressure on a country already embroiled in conflict along its southern border.
“My neighbors and friends are bunkering for November but starting to get concerned about flight disruptions over the holidays,” said a 36-year-old American in Saudi Arabia, comparing it to the Covid era. “A lot of offices have moved to virtual or have reduced staff and remote learning is in place.”
Elsewhere in the region, other international gatherings remain on track, though the risk remains that they could be disrupted if the U.S. launches strikes in the coming week.
In Abu Dhabi, where no attacks have been recorded since May, two U.S. oil firms canceled plans for their executives to attend one of the region’s biggest energy conferences, citing security concerns, Reuters reported. The event will proceed as scheduled next week with “strong” U.S. participation and more than 120 American exhibiting companies, the organizer, DMG, told Reuters.
The conference is expected to host nearly 240,000 people, according to the organizers.
In Bahrain, one of the worst-hit countries by Iran this year, people said they still felt the psychological impact of the war.
“There is still that traumatic effect,” 21-year-old Fawaz told CNN. “When you hear the bombings, it’s kind of like you feel it in your hearts and it’s hard to sleep at night, especially when there are bombings outside.”
“A lot of people have become used to it by now, but it’s still very scary,” he added.
Despite growing anxiety over the possible resumption of war, there has been a flurry of quiet diplomacy over the past week.
U.S. Vice President JD Vance sent Iran’s top security official Mohsen Rezaei a letter, which the Islamic Republic is reviewing, according to Iranian media. Trump has claimed the letter related to an Iranian request for medical supplies, but it has raised hopes that a diplomatic breakthrough could still be possible.
Iranian officials are in Qatar for talks, a Qatari official said. Qatar has played a prominent role in mediating, but the official added there was no U.S. delegation present Saturday.
On Monday, Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said the ball is “entirely in the U.S.’ court,” as “exchanges of messages” between Washington and Tehran were ongoing, according to Iran’s state news agency, IRNA. Baghaei doubled down on Tehran’s demand that “no agreement can be reached,” nor the key Strait of Hormuz reopened, as long as the U.S. naval blockade on Iranian ports remains.

articles.title_orig: Palantir reports booming U.S. commercial revenue growth, topping government for first time
articles.title_zh: Palantir reports booming U.S. commercial revenue growth, topping government for first time
articles.content_orig:
Palantir beat Wall Street's third-quarter estimates after the bell on Monday, with U.S. commercial revenue topping government for the first time as businesses adopt more of the company's artificial intelligence tools.
Shares dipped about 3% in extended trading.
Here's how the company did compared to LSEG estimates:
Revenue nearly doubled from a year ago and blew past $2 billion for the first time ever, Palantir said. Net income more than doubled to $1.13 billion, or 44 cents per share, from about $476 million, or 18 cents per share.
"I don't believe anyone's had consistent results like this in the history of software AI, ever," CEO Alex Karp told CNBC's Seema Mody in an interview, adding that the business is succeeding without salespeople.
Palantir has long been known for its strength in the government sector, but its commercial segment caught up in Q3.
U.S. commercial revenue jumped 148% to $984 million, surpassing U.S. government revenue of $953 million, which was up 96%. The company's U.S. commercial revenue has more than quintupled over the last two years.
Palantir lifted its guidance, saying it now expects U.S. commercial revenue "in excess of" $3.56 billion for the full year. Last quarter, the company boosted its forecast to $3.42 billion. The company projects about $2.65 billion in revenue for the fourth quarter and about $8.53 billion for full-year 2026.
Karp has openly supported the use of open-weight models and criticized leading AI labs, which he told CNBC earlier this year are forcing businesses to sell their data sovereignty. Karp, on Monday, also reiterated recent calls to nationalize AI labs, calling it the "only realistic way" to manage liability.
In September, Karp joined major tech CEOs at the White House as calls for regulation mounted following claims from AI researchers that the technology has a more than 10% of killing humanity .
"My message to everybody is: Beware of thinking you can delay the future in AI," he told CNBC. "The future is here. The political ramifications of it are here."

articles.title_orig: Explorer Gadget Gets a Major Upgrade, Alongside New Quality-of-Life Updates
articles.title_zh: Explorer Gadget Gets a Major Upgrade, Alongside New Quality-of-Life Updates
articles.content_orig:
The Explorer Gadget now works while you play, alongside a redesigned catch summary, faster Pokémon appraisal, and several gameplay improvements.
The Explorer Gadget is getting a useful upgrade in Pokémon GO! Trainers can now use it to automatically catch Pokémon and spin PokéStops while actively playing the game , rather than only when Pokémon GO is running in the background.
Alongside the Explorer Gadget improvements, several quality-of-life updates have recently rolled out, including a redesigned catch summary, a dedicated Appraise button, clearer PokéStop visuals, and changes to Power Spot encounters.
Here’s what’s new and how it works.
Previously, the Explorer Gadget could automatically attempt to catch Pokémon and spin PokéStops while Pokémon GO wasn’t actively open on your device. With this update, it can now do both while you’re playing, much like a Pokémon GO Plus + accessory.
Trainers level 20 and above can activate the Explorer Gadget by tapping its icon in the top-right corner of the Map View or finding it under Key Items in the Item Bag.
When active, a pink Poké Ball icon will appear above Pokémon or PokéStops that the Explorer Gadget is attempting to interact with.
You can still catch Pokémon or spin PokéStops yourself while the Explorer Gadget is active.
Simply tap the Pokémon or PokéStop that the Gadget is targeting to take over the interaction. However, you’ll only have a limited window of time to do so once the pink Poké Ball icon appears.
There are a few important restrictions to keep in mind:
Trainers can review which Pokémon the Explorer Gadget caught and how many PokéStops it spun by opening the Explorer Gadget from the Map View or the Key Items section of the Item Bag.
If you’re unfamiliar with this feature, check out our Explorer Gadget guide for more information.
The Explorer Gadget isn’t the only thing getting attention. Pokémon GO has also rolled out several smaller gameplay and interface improvements.
The screen displayed after catching a Pokémon has been redesigned, with clearer visuals for catch rewards and bonuses. This should make it easier to see exactly what you earned from each catch.
Checking a Pokémon’s IVs is now easier! A dedicated Appraise button has been added to Pokémon summary screens, just above the Additional Options button.
This removes the need to open the Additional Options menu every time you want to appraise a Pokémon.
Visiting a Power Spot or placing a Pokémon at a Power Spot after winning a Max Battle will no longer trigger special wild encounters around the Power Spot.
According to Pokémon GO, this change is intended to improve the consistency of wild encounters for all players.
The visual rings surrounding wild Pokémon attracted by Lure Modules or encountered while exploring Routes have been updated.
Spun PokéStops now have adjusted color saturation, making them easier to distinguish from unspun PokéStops.
This is a welcome accessibility improvement, particularly for Trainers who have difficulty distinguishing between similar colors.
The visual effects surrounding Pokémon attracted by the Mystery Box or Coin Bag have also been refreshed.
These are relatively small changes individually, but together they should make everyday Pokémon GO gameplay a little more convenient.

articles.title_orig: US petrol prices dip ahead of midterms as voters eye costs
articles.title_zh: US petrol prices dip ahead of midterms as voters eye costs
articles.content_orig:
Petrol prices have dipped amid renewed diplomatic efforts to end the US-Israel war on Iran, but remain high ahead of the United States midterm elections , as the cost of living remains a central issue for voters.
On Monday, the average price for a gallon (3.78 litres) of regular petrol was $4.17, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), which tracks daily petrol prices. That is down 12 cents from this time last week and 23 cents from a month ago.
By comparison, prices were $3.04 this time a year ago and $2.98 on February 28, when the US and Israel first struck Iran.
Diesel fuel prices remain high at $6.29 per gallon, but that is down 6 cents from this time last week. Diesel prices climbed above $6 a gallon for the first time in September before topping out at $6.53.
The average petrol price of President Donald Trump’s second term to date was set to exceed $3.46 a gallon on Monday, surpassing the previous record for a presidential administration set under former President Joe Biden, according to a Financial Times analysis of federal data.
Oil prices are continuing to fall, down 6 percent on Monday as diplomatic efforts to end the US-Israel war on Iran continued following in-person talks in Qatar over the weekend.
“Oil markets down significantly this morning after Trump signalled he favoured negotiations and not new attacks on Iran,” Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, said in a post on X. “Oil down [approximately] 5%, wholesale gasoline and diesel pointing to roughly 16 [cents per gallon] decline. The national average could fall under $4 a gallon in the next week barring a course change.”
Cost-of-living issues remain top of mind for US voters as they head to the polls. An Associated Press-NORC poll last month found that a majority of Americans believe addressing cost-of-living issues should be a priority for Congress, including 78 percent of Republicans and 89 percent of Democrats.
“Once this conflict comes to an end, gas prices will drop drastically, and the Iranian terrorist regime will not have a nuclear weapon,” White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers told Al Jazeera. “Protecting America’s national security from threats by a radical terrorist regime that has chanted ‘Death to America’ for 47 years was the right thing to do – and President Trump is the only president who has had the courage to do it.”
Rogers added, “Thanks to the exceptional work of the US military, more oil is now flowing out of the Persian Gulf than before the Iran conflict began.”
On Wall Street, oil and gas giant stocks were trending downward in midday trading. ConocoPhillips was down 3.7 percent, Chevron 2.3 percent and ExxonMobil 3.3 percent.
The major US indices more broadly were in positive territory. The Nasdaq was up 0.7 percent, the S&P 500 0.6 percent and the Dow Jones Industrial Average 1 percent.

articles.title_orig: One of Google’s Android partners turned 1.3 million set-top boxes into a botnet
articles.title_zh: One of Google’s Android partners turned 1.3 million set-top boxes into a botnet
articles.content_orig:
Google says a manufacturer ‘intentionally’ hijacked its devices with malware.
Google says a manufacturer ‘intentionally’ hijacked its devices with malware.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
Google says one of its Android manufacturing partners secretly built a backdoor in 1.3 million devices and turned them into a botnet. The company says it has now dismantled the backdoor and “cut ties” with the manufacturer, the Shenzhen, China-based Videostrong Technology Co., which has been banned from building or selling certified Android devices or supplying software for them.
The infected devices were used without owners’ knowledge for “malicious activity,” like ad fraud, data exfiltration, and routing unauthorized network traffic. Google claims the “backdoor and botnet were intentionally developed, deployed, and operated for financial gain,” saying:
Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices. These secondary modules were conducting ad-fraud; silently enrolling infected devices into residential proxy networks; and loading additional malware onto XCPE-compromised devices. We also took action to disrupt the command and control (C2) domains that operate these affiliate modules. Because these affiliates each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE, we assess that taking down their C2 domains will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices.
It wasn’t just one device that was impacted, either — the malware was found “built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years.” Most of those were Android TV set-top boxes, but the botnet also infected other “Android-based IoT devices, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and digital signage devices.”
Google says Videostrong used “obfuscation techniques” to load the malware onto users’ devices after they booted up the hardware for the first time. Google also says it made changes to its review process for device manufacturers after this incident.

articles.title_orig: Israel Turns to Next Big Question: Who Gets a Shot at Being Prime Minister?
articles.title_zh: Israel Turns to Next Big Question: Who Gets a Shot at Being Prime Minister?
articles.content_orig:
President Isaac Herzog will begin consultations with representatives of the parties elected to the 26th Knesset on Wednesday, starting with the smallest factions in an unusual departure from previous rounds of coalition negotiations, the President's Office announced on Monday.
Rather than beginning with the largest parties, Herzog will invite faction representatives in ascending order of Knesset seats, beginning with Religious Zionism-Zehut and concluding with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud on Thursday evening.
According to the President's Office, the decision is intended to "encourage thinking outside the box," allowing Herzog to consider a wider range of potential coalition arrangements before consulting with the larger factions.
The consultations come as Israel's political parties face the challenge of forming a governing coalition following the October 27 election, with neither of the two largest parties, Likud and Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar, enjoying a straightforward path to a 61-seat majority.
Herzog has emphasized the importance of exploring potential compromises to prevent another election, with the unusual consultation order potentially allowing smaller factions to present alternative coalition arrangements before the president meets with Netanyahu and Eisenkot.
In his statement, Herzog said he would hear the positions of all factions, seeking to "exhaust every possibility, broaden the dialogue, and explore any avenue that could advance the process."
The president also left open the possibility of holding a second round of consultations if necessary.
The consultations will begin Wednesday at 5 p.m. with Religious Zionism-Zehut, followed by Shas at 6:15 p.m. and Yisrael Beytenu at 7:30 p.m.
Meetings will resume Thursday morning, beginning with United Torah Judaism at 8:30 a.m., followed by Otzma Yehudit at 9:45 a.m., the Democrats at 11 a.m., and Ra'am at 12:15 p.m.
Following an afternoon break, Herzog will meet with the Joint List at 4:45 p.m., B'Yachad at 6 p.m., Yashar at 7:15 p.m., and finally Likud at 8:30 p.m.
During the consultations, each faction will be given an opportunity to recommend a Knesset member to receive the mandate to form the next government.
While the number of recommendations each candidate receives matters, the president is not legally required to select the candidate with the most recommendations. Instead, Herzog must determine which Knesset member has the best chance of successfully forming a government.
Under Basic Law: The Government, the Knesset member entrusted with forming a government has 28 days to assemble a coalition. The president may grant an extension of up to 14 additional days if necessary.
Should the designated candidate fail to form a government, the law provides for further procedures that could see another Knesset member given the opportunity to assemble a coalition.
The consultations will be broadcast live on the president's official social media accounts, allowing the public to follow the parties' recommendations and the opening stages of the coalition-building process.

articles.title_orig: Yemen's Houthis advance to within 80 km of Aden, sources say
articles.title_zh: Yemen's Houthis advance to within 80 km of Aden, sources say
articles.content_orig:
Al-Jawf has become a new focal point in the conflict between forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognised government and the Houthis, highlighting the strategic importance of the northern governorate.
A major counteroffensive has been launched by the Yemeni government army and forces loyal to it to capture the strategic heights east of the provincial capital, al-Hazm, from the Houthis.
The operations are part of Operation Dawn of Yemen, launched by the government last month to reverse Houthi territorial gains and restore state control in the country.
Al-Hazm has become a central part of this operation, with the city a potential launchpad for government forces against the Houthis. They have controlled the capital Sanaa and most of northern Yemen since the war broke out in September 2014.
During the 12 years of war in Yemen, control over al-Hazm has shifted several times, with the Houthis seizing the city in March 2020.
The governorate remains highly coveted due to its expansive border with Saudi Arabia and its direct geographic links to five pivotal governorates: Hadramout, Saada, Sanaa, Amran and oil-rich Marib and close to the capital, Sanaa.
Al-Jawf also acts as a vital defensive shield for Marib, controlled by government forces, preventing the Houthis from advancing into the eastern regions. It is also a gateway to major Houthi strongholds in northern Yemen.
Field Commander Colonel Rabie Al-Qurashi said government forces have been able to win complete control over the strategic Huwaishan mountain range, east of al-Hazm city. He said it is the first line of defence for the Houthis in the eastern axis and control over the rugged region would give government forces the ability to disrupt rebel supply routes.
“Government forces succeeded in breaking that defensive format with partial control over the Al-Alam front road,” Al-Qurashi said. “The government advance represents a beginning to tighten the noose on the Houthis in the upper al-Labanat camp,” which is regarded as a vital eastern gateway to Sanaa.
Ali Al-Dahab, a military and strategic affairs researcher, said there are immense tactical benefits from holding this elevated terrain.
“The recent advances of government forces in Al-Jawf are a military transformation that serves the course of future operations for their arrival to al-Hazm city,” Al-Dahab told Al Jazeera.
“The government forces’ recovery of a number of heights there provides a military and psychological morale advantage and confuses the Houthis’ decisions, in addition to granting government forces monitoring, movement, and observation of Houthi supply lines and securing their own lines.”
Military spokesman Majed Abdullah Al-Nuzaili said on X that recent military operations against Houthi positions in al-Jawf were “inflicting losses on the militia’s capabilities”.
The government dominates the vast eastern desert district of Khabb wa ash Sha’af, representing 82 percent of the governorate’s total area. The Houthis control the provincial capital, al-Hazm, and 10 other districts.
Security and political affairs researcher Brigadier General Ahmed Al-Awadhi stressed the importance of “continuous but not rapid” government advances in the area.
“The advances of government forces in Al-Jawf cannot be ignored or their importance underestimated,” Al-Awadhi told Al Jazeera.
“Control over heights or mountain ranges in the desert Al-Jawf governorate represents points of military strength regardless of their proximity to or distance from the governorate capital.”
The government forces advances in al-Jawf highlight a historical vulnerability for the Houthis, having suffered repeated defeats in battles in desert and open areas, he added.
The developments coincide with the Presidential Council’s appointment of Major General Amin Ali Al-Akimi as governor and military commander of al-Jawf.
“[His] reappointment… comes within the context of restructuring the theatre of operations and unifying the front,” Ibrahim Jalal, a Yemen-focused analyst told Al Jazeera.
“Hailing from Dhu Hussein, a branch of the Daham Bakil tribe, Al-Akimi possesses tribal and military influence that could help mobilise tribes, overcome divisions and bolster momentum on the ground. However, translating this influence into sustainable gains remains contingent upon unifying command and control, coordinating operations across all battlefronts, securing military and logistical support and strengthening anti-corruption efforts to improve the efficient management of military resources.”
The Houthis say they have thwarted advances by government forces in al-Jawf and Marib.
Fighting has continued in other parts of Yemen as Houthi-affiliated media reported air strikes on an oil company facility in the Bajil district of Hodeidah, which coincide with fierce fighting further south.
Government forces repelled Houthi attacks in al-Aqroudh and on the Tur al-Baha front in Lahij governorate. Intense fighting continues in Taiz governorate.
The siege of Taiz City continues to strain medical infrastructure, with deliveries of food and fuel severely restricted. Civilians remain at risk from sniper fire from surrounding hillsides, authorities have warned.
Governor Nabil Shamsan said that hospitals are working at only 20 percent capacity, with 120 health centres entirely shut due to the siege.
“We urge the international community to secure at least one safe route between Taiz and Aden to enable citizen movement and the smooth entry of services, essential materials and goods,” Shamsan appealed to Al Jazeera.
More than 300,000 people have fled their homes in western Yemen due to the escalating fighting, leaving civilians highly vulnerable.

articles.title_orig: Marvell doubles down on AI boom with costly $115 billion Lumentum deal
articles.title_zh: Marvell doubles down on AI boom with costly $115 billion Lumentum deal
articles.content_orig:
Marvell Technology Chairman and CEO Matt Murphy and Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston detail their record-breaking merger and how their ‘shared vision’ will create a category leader in AI connectivity on ‘The Claman Countdown.’
Marvell Technology chairman and CEO Matt Murphy said the chipmaker’s historic $115 billion acquisition of Lumentum is a "once in a generation’ opportunity to unite two of the most dominating companies in the AI boom and create a "category leader."
Appearing alongside Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston on "The Claman Countdown," Murphy detailed the companies’ record-breaking merger on Monday, predicting that the transaction will cement Marvell’s position at the forefront of AI connectivity.
"It's very rare that you can find two companies of the caliber of Lumentum and Marvell that are number one in their respective areas that find a moment in time where you can combine and create a category leader in a new category," he told anchor Liz Claman.
AMERICA AND CHINA ARE FIGHTING FOR THE FUTURE OF AI — CHIPS ARE THE BATTLEFIELD
The race to build AI infrastructure is accelerating as concerns grow over centralized technological power. (Noah Berger / Getty Images)
"This AI connectivity is going to be as consequential as… the compute category, or the memory category, the fab category, and the IP licensing category."
Murphy's comments follow the announcement of Marvell’s agreement to acquire Lumentum in a landmark $115 billion transaction, marking the largest merger between two publicly traded companies. The deal will unite two massive AI enablers, equipped with electrical and optical expertise, to address connectivity requirements for next-generation AI infrastructure .
MASSIVE AI BOOM PUTS ONE OF AMERICA’S OLDEST MANUFACTURERS ON PATH TO DOUBLE IN SIZE, CEO SAYS
"Both companies.are executing phenomenally well. And what we see, Liz, is a multiplying effect, where we're gonna do much better together in two years than we would on a standalone basis," Hurlston predicted.
Under the terms of the all-stock agreement, Lumentum shareholders will receive 4.5 shares of Marvell common stock for each share held, according to Marvell’s announcement.
"It’s really a historic day for the two companies," Murphy said. "We're putting together basically the best-in-class leader in AI connectivity technology for semiconductors with the leader in photonics. And it is something that hasn't been done before."
Marvell Technology Chairman and CEO Matt Murphy (Right) appeared alongside Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston (Left) on "The Claman Countdown" on Monday. (Left (Takaaki Iwabu/Bloomberg via Getty Images), Right (Lam Yik Fei/Bloomberg via Getty Images) / Getty Images)
Marvell designs artificial intelligence chips and technology that powers data centers , while Lumentum designs lasers and other optical components that use light to transmit data between chips and servers.
Murphy said Lumentum and Marvell, both headquartered in Northern California, have a "shared vision" and detailed how he believes the two tech companies will work better together than apart.
IT TOOK 3 MONTHS TO GET INSIDE THIS MASSIVE TEXAS DATA CENTER — HERE’S WHAT WE SAW
"Together, because of the additional opportunity we see with each other, there's an opportunity to really outperform as a combined company," the Marvell CEO said.
Murphy, who said the merger has received "tremendous support" from hyperscalers, told FOX Business that he expects "significant" revenue synergies and other benefits once the companies are joined together.
AI chip giant Nvidia is a strategic investor in both Lumentum, which has a market value of around $76 billion, and Marvell, with a value of roughly $172 billion.
The Marvell-Lumentum deal has garnered "super positive" feedback from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Hurlston said. (Getty )
CLICK HERE TO GET FOX BUSINESS ON THE GO
Hurlston told FOX Business that Murphy discussed the potential Lumentum acquisition with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang early in the process, adding that reaction from Nvidia has been "super positive."
"Nvidia is invested in Marvell, Nvidia is invested in Lumentum. We think we can actually bring a lot more product to bear to Nvidia a lot more quickly in this combination," Hurlston said.

articles.title_orig: Snap settles with two teens during trial testing claims social media caused depression, eating disorders
articles.title_zh: Snap settles with two teens during trial testing claims social media caused depression, eating disorders
articles.content_orig:
Snapchat parent Snap Inc has reached a settlement during a trial over claims brought by two teenagers who say the company designed the platform to be addictive, causing their depression, anxiety and eating disorders, attorneys for the plaintiffs said on Monday.
Jury selection began last week for the trial, the second in Los Angeles state court over claims brought by young people who say they became addicted to social media after Snap, Meta Platforms, TikTok and Alphabet's YouTube designed their platforms to encourage compulsive use.
The plaintiffs had previously settled with Meta, TikTok and YouTube.
"Our ultimate goal is to hold these social media companies accountable for how their actions have impacted millions of children across the country, and these settlements allow us to keep building toward that goal," John Morgan and Emily Jeffcott, trial attorneys for plaintiff K.D.B., said in a statement.
The trial was set to be the first for Snap in the sweeping litigation over social media's impact on teens, after the company settled the other cases that had been scheduled for trial. The company's chief executive, Evan Spiegel, had been expected to testify.
The case had been selected from thousands of pending lawsuits as a bellwether intended to test the claims against Snap and the other companies and potentially influence how similar cases are resolved. The next bellwether trials are scheduled to begin in March, according to the plaintiffs' lawyers.
A Snap spokesperson said in a statement that the company has built safeguards, launched safety tutorials and partnered with experts, and remains committed to “continually strengthening the safety, privacy, and well-being of our community."
Plaintiffs S.J., a 16-year-old girl from Illinois, and K.D.B., an 18-year-old from Mississippi, say they began using YouTube as early as age 3 and the other platforms around age 9, developing compulsive habits they blame on features such as autoplay and infinite scroll.
The companies have rejected claims their platforms were designed to addict young people, and say they have taken action to make the apps safe places for young people to express themselves.
Social media companies face thousands of lawsuits in federal and state courts brought by individuals, school districts, municipalities and other government entities alleging the companies knowingly sought to addict children to their platforms, contributing to a youth mental health crisis involving anxiety, depression and suicide.
In the first case to go to trial, which ended in March, a Los Angeles jury found Meta and YouTube had been negligent and awarded a young woman $6 million in damages.
The next two teens whose cases were selected for trials either settled or dropped their claims against the companies.
The first school district chosen for trial settled with all of the companies.
In August, Meta struck settlements worth up to $18 billion with nearly every state and US territory to resolve lawsuits brought by attorneys general over claims its platforms harmed teens and agreed to make changes to how Instagram and Facebook work for teens. The deal conditioned $5 billion of the payout on the states reaching similar settlements with Snap, TikTok and YouTube.
